ba-ba-de-shou-ji-xian-shui-yi-hui-er: Lele joined three cardboard boxes into a long tunnel. His blue toy car was waiting for its very first trip.
‘Dad, you can be the driver!’ Dad sat on the rug and took the car. Lele hurried to the far end of the tunnel.
Ding! Dad's phone rang. He glanced down, and the car stayed at the entrance. It did not come through.
‘Is it here yet?’ Lele asked. ‘Just a moment,’ Dad said, still moving his finger across the screen.
Lele lifted the exit a little. ‘There's a hill here.’ ‘That looks lovely,’ Dad said without looking up.
Lele slowly lowered the box. ‘You didn't see it.’ He took the car back and sat very still.
At last, Dad looked up. He looked at the tunnel and then at Lele. ‘You were waiting to play together, but I kept looking at my phone.’
‘I waited lots of times,’ Lele said. Dad nodded. ‘I'm sorry. I'd like to start this trip again, from the entrance.’
They found a little basket. Lele lined it with a soft cloth. ‘The phone can have a little sleep here.’
Dad set a fifteen-minute reminder and turned on Do Not Disturb. ‘This is our building time. Important calls will have their own ring.’
This time, the car really went into the tunnel. Rumble, rumble! Lele crawled beside it, all the way to the exit.
The exit was too low, and the car got stuck. Dad lay down to look. ‘Oh! The roof is almost touching the top of the car.’
Lele chose two taller blocks. Dad held the box steady, and the car delivered a wooden bead safely to the station.
Suddenly, the special ring sounded. After the call, Dad said, ‘Grandma is downstairs with the groceries. I need to help carry them.’
‘But we haven't finished.’ Lele held the car tightly. Dad crouched down. ‘That's true. Would you like to stay here, or come and meet Grandma?’
Lele wanted to go too. They left the tunnel on the rug and agreed to make one more delivery when they came back.
Back home, Dad put the groceries away and returned his phone to the basket. ‘The driver is back! Where's our next stop?’
Lele turned the exit toward Dad. ‘The next stop is over there.’ This time, when he looked up, Dad was looking right back.
men-kou-de-zai-jian-xiao-yi-shi: An osmanthus tree grew by the kindergarten gate. Every morning, Duoduo slowed down when she reached it.
Other children walked inside with their backpacks. Duoduo held Mama's hand more tightly. ‘Can you come in with me today?’
Mama crouched down. ‘You wish we could stay together a little longer.’ Duoduo nodded, and tears fell onto her cardigan.
Her teacher came over without taking her hand. ‘Yesterday's little bridge is still by the window. When you're ready, I'll go and look with you.’
‘Today I'll say goodbye at the gate,’ Mama said. ‘I'll come back after your afternoon snack. Your teacher will stay with you here.’
‘One more hug,’ Duoduo said. Mama opened her arms and gently held her. The little duck on her backpack nestled between them.
Together, they made a plan: one hug, one palm-to-palm touch, and one wave. After those three little things, they would say goodbye.
Duoduo waved, then wanted to run after Mama. Her teacher crouched beside her. ‘You're missing Mama. We can stand here for a little while.’
Mama turned to wave from their agreed spot, then kept walking. She did not slip away secretly or keep coming back.
Duoduo was still crying. Her teacher sat with her by the window and offered a tissue. The little bridge stood nearby.
A wooden car rolled over the bridge. Duoduo reached out and caught it at the other end.
‘It needs a road here,’ she whispered. Her teacher moved the blocks closer. ‘Where would you like the road to go?’
The road reached a little house. Duoduo played for a while, then missed Mama again. She asked her teacher to look out of the window with her.
After the afternoon snack, Mama came back. Duoduo ran over. ‘I cried, and I built a really long road!’
Mama welcomed her into her arms. ‘So today had tears and a long road. You can tell me about both.’
The next morning, Duoduo still felt a little sad to say goodbye. She held up her palm. ‘Can we do it just like yesterday?’
One hug, one touch, and one wave. Duoduo wiped her eyes and walked toward the window with her teacher.
The bridge was still there. Duoduo put a car on it. ‘Today it's going a little farther.’
mei-mei-lai-le-wo-hai-zai-zhe-li: After the baby came home, a little cot appeared in the living room. Xiaohe's red chair was moved beside the curtains.
‘Look, she's yawning!’ ‘Look, she's holding my finger!’ Xiaohe held his cardboard train and waited for everyone to turn around.
Dad wanted a family photo. ‘Xiaohe, stand beside your sister.’ Xiaohe stayed where he was and hid the train behind his back.
‘Is she the only one you want to look at?’ Xiaohe asked. Mama put down the little towel and turned toward him.
‘We've been so busy with your sister,’ Mama said. ‘You wanted to show us your train, and your red chair was moved away too.’
Xiaohe's mouth trembled. ‘I want to sit beside you too. I don't want to wait every day.’
Mama patted the place beside her. ‘Come here.’ Xiaohe sat down and rested his head against her arm for a long time.
Dad brought back the red chair and cleared a low shelf for the train. ‘This space is for the things you make.’
They agreed that Dad would build a station with Xiaohe after dinner. Mama would care for the baby if she needed them then.
On the first evening, Xiaohe had just put up the roof when the baby cried. Dad started to stand, then looked at Mama.
Mama picked up the baby. ‘I'll take this turn.’ Dad sat back beside the red chair. ‘Station master, which roof block do we need?’
Xiaohe handed Dad the last block. The bright, roomy station could finally hold his long train.
Sometimes Xiaohe still said, ‘I don't like my sister right now.’ Dad listened. ‘Was the waiting too long again today?’
Dad asked, ‘Would you like me beside you, or some time on your own?’ ‘Just sit here first,’ Xiaohe said. ‘Please don't go.’
A few days later, the baby lay awake looking up. Xiaohe brought a big sheet of blue paper. ‘Would she like to see my station too?’
Mama held the paper safely outside the cot so the baby could see. Xiaohe made a train sound. ‘Whooo!’ His sister moved one little foot.
‘Shall we take a photo today?’ Xiaohe asked. ‘I want to hold my train.’ Dad smiled. ‘You can choose where to sit.’
In the photo, the baby rested against Mama and Xiaohe sat on his red chair. His long train stretched from his hands toward everyone.
wo-men-jia-de-zan-ting-shou-shi: On Friday evening, Anan put her green backpack beside the table. She wanted to pack a magnifying glass and look for leaves at the park.
Mama wanted to visit Grandma, and Dad wanted to go to the park. ‘We visited last week.’ ‘But we planned this outing already.’
Both hurried to say the next thing. The tea on the table stopped steaming, but their voices grew louder.
Anan hugged her backpack. ‘Maybe I won't look for leaves.’ Her voice was as small as a button hidden inside the bag.
Mama stopped. Dad lowered his hands too. ‘Did our voices make you feel worried?’ Anan nodded.
‘You don't have to give up your wish to stop our argument,’ Mama said. ‘Making plans together is something grown-ups need to practise too.’
Dad opened his palm. ‘I need a short pause and some water.’ Mama nodded. The table grew a little quieter.
Dad told Anan, ‘I'll sit by the window for five minutes, then come back. Would you like to stay here, or draw with Mama?’
Anan wanted to draw a big leaf. Mama helped find the crayons. She did not ask Anan to persuade Dad or decide who was right.
Five minutes later, Dad returned. ‘I interrupted you earlier. Please finish telling me why you want to visit Grandma. I'll listen.’
‘Her new glasses are ready,’ Mama said. ‘I want to help her check how they fit.’ This time, Dad did not rush to answer.
Dad said, ‘I remember promising Anan the park. I didn't want to change that again.’ Anan looked up from her drawing.
‘We were each thinking only about our own part,’ Mama said. She put the two wishes together and thought again.
They checked when Grandma was free, then planned to visit in the morning and spend a little time at a nearby park that afternoon.
‘Will two stops make you tired?’ Dad asked. Anan thought. ‘The park doesn't have to be big. It just needs leaves.’
Before bed, they made a plan: anyone could say ‘pause’ or open a palm when the voices became too hurried. Then they would agree when to talk again.
The next day, Grandma wore her new glasses to admire Anan's big leaf. That afternoon, a real leaf landed on their picnic blanket.
Anan put it in her backpack. Mama and Dad were still planning dinner, but this time she heard one whole sentence, then the next.
na-ge-yue-ding-mei-you-zuo-dao: On Wednesday, Dad said, ‘I'll take you to the puppet show on Sunday.’ Lele stuck a little star on the calendar.
On Thursday, he asked whether puppets could blink. On Friday, he packed his little handkerchief in his orange backpack.
On Sunday, he put his shoes on early. Dad took out his phone to book tickets, then stopped. ‘This show has sold out.’
Lele looked at the star on the calendar. ‘But you promised.’ He kept his backpack on.
Dad quickly said, ‘Shall we have your favourite noodles instead?’ Lele shook his head. ‘Today I wanted the puppet show.’
Dad put down his phone. ‘You're right. I forgot to book the tickets early. You remembered correctly. I didn't take care of what I promised.’
‘I've waited so many days.’ Lele's tears fell, one after another. Dad sat beside him without suggesting more fun places.
After a while, Lele asked, ‘Is there really no way to see it today?’ Dad checked carefully, then gently nodded.
‘I'm sorry,’ Dad said. ‘I'd like to make it up to you. You're still upset, and you don't have to say it's all right now.’
Lele squeezed his handkerchief. ‘I still want to see the puppet that sings.’ Dad asked, ‘Would you like to look at the next show?’
This time, Dad checked the date, made sure they could go, and bought the tickets. Lele sat beside him until it was all done.
They put another star on the following Sunday. Dad noted when to leave too. ‘I'll be responsible for reminding us.’
There was still a long afternoon ahead. ‘I'd like to stay home first,’ Lele said. Dad helped him hang his backpack on its little hook.
Someone cycled past the window. Lele found two socks and added paper eyes. ‘This puppet doesn't know how to sing yet.’
Dad sang a line in a low voice. Lele smiled a little, then said, ‘But I still want to go to the theatre.’
‘I remember,’ Dad said. The following week, he had the tickets ready and called Lele to leave at the time they had agreed.
The theatre lights dimmed, and a puppet peeped from a little window. Lele nudged Dad. ‘It really can blink!’
Lele sang like the puppet all the way home. By the old calendar star, Dad said, ‘Thank you for telling me how disappointed you felt.’
sheng-zi-shua-de-yi-sheng: Xiaoman's rope swished over her head, then under her feet. Anan hugged her yellow rope. ‘I want to jump like that too.’
She swung hard, and the rope landed in front of her toes. Before her feet could jump, her hands hurried into another turn.
The rope caught beside her shoe. Anan stopped. ‘My feet are always one step late.’ Mama helped lay the rope flat.
Mama asked her to stand on the middle of the rope and adjusted its length to fit her. When Anan tried again, there was no long extra length trailing behind.
‘We don't need to jump continuously yet,’ Mama said. Anan put the rope behind her and slowly swung it forward, waiting for it to land by her feet.
Once it was still, she stepped gently over it. One swing, one step. Xiaoman left plenty of room beside her.
On their next visit, Anan put down the rope and tried little jumps. Her shoes rose just above the ground and landed in the same place.
She did not jump very high or move forward. Mama copied her. ‘Like one little kernel of corn making a gentle pop.’
Anan picked up the rope again. It swung from behind her. When it was almost at her feet, she made a little jump.
Swish! The rope went through. Anan landed steadily and opened her eyes wide. ‘I jumped over it!’
The next time, the rope touched her shoe again. Anan felt discouraged. ‘I could do it just now. Why can't I do it again?’
Mama asked, ‘When it felt smooth, how did your hands and feet wait for each other?’ Anan slowed down and found that little moment again.
Her arms felt tired. The three of them sat in the shade to drink water. The yellow rope curved on the ground like a quiet stream.
Another afternoon, Anan tried going on without stopping. The first jump worked, but the rope slowed on the second. She stood steadily and began again.
Xiaoman did not call, ‘Go faster!’ She simply let Anan hear her own rope touching the ground. Swish, swish, swish.
Anan tried her own rhythm. One, two, three! After the third jump, she smiled and stopped the rope.
On the way home, Mama asked if she wanted any more jumps. Anan shook her head. ‘That's enough today. Next time, I want to find that swishing sound again.’
The yellow rope hung by the door. As Anan passed, she gently touched a handle. Those three swishes were something she had learnt, little by little.
lan-qiu-dong-dong-hui-lai-le: On the court, Ayuan walked along, bouncing his ball with a steady thump. Lele listened. It sounded like a little marching band.
Lele picked up a big basketball. Before he could spread his fingers, it slipped toward his tummy. It was heavier than he expected.
Dad found a ball that fitted smaller hands. Lele hugged it. ‘I can hold this one firmly.’
He wanted to walk and bounce at once. His feet ran forward and his hand pushed sideways. The ball rolled toward a bench far away.
‘It won't come with me.’ Lele fetched it and hugged it again. Dad asked, ‘Shall we stay here and listen to one bounce first?’
Lele placed his feet a little apart and gently bent his knees. He sent the ball down. Thump! It rose, and he caught it with both hands.
He tried again. This time, the ball bounced toward his shoe. Lele looked down. ‘I pushed it sideways that time.’
Dad showed him: open the hand, let the fingers spread naturally, and gently press the ball downward. When it comes back, let the hand move with it.
Lele tried without hitting so hard. One bounce, then catch. Another bounce, then catch. More often now, the ball returned to his hands.
When the ball rose, he gently sent it down again. Thump, thump! He missed the third bounce, and the ball stopped by his feet.
Lele hugged the ball and laughed. ‘There were two thumps!’ Dad smiled. ‘You waited for it to come back before the next bounce.’
After a while, his hands felt tired. Lele put the ball beside his feet, then went with Dad to the bench for water.
On their second visit, Lele hurried and the ball ran away again. He brought it back and began with one bounce and one catch.
As he slowed down, the ball seemed to recognise his hand. One, two, three. Lele's feet stayed in place.
Ayuan came over and stood in another clear space. Their ball sounds sometimes matched and sometimes took turns.
Lele bounced five times in a row and caught the ball. Ayuan asked if he wanted to try walking. ‘I'd like to practise standing steadily first,’ Lele said.
While Dad put the empty water bottle away, Lele tried another short turn. This time, he listened less to the count and watched when the ball came back.
On the way home, the ball rested in its net bag. Lele tapped his knees softly. Thump, thump. They could play again tomorrow.
xiao-che-lun-man-man-zhuan: The mint-green bicycle stood in the courtyard. Xiaohe touched its bell. ‘Can it take me a long way?’ ‘Let's begin right here,’ Dad said.
Dad adjusted the seat. When Xiaohe sat down, both feet could reach the ground firmly. Dad checked the helmet strap too.
‘How do I stop after I start?’ Xiaohe asked. Dad helped him squeeze the brakes and try them while pushing the bicycle.
The bicycle stopped. Dad pointed to the tree's shadow. ‘Today we'll practise on this flat space, with no vehicles. We won't go onto the road.’
Xiaohe left the pedals alone at first and gently pushed forward with both feet. Dad walked beside him, leaving room for his feet to land.
Before the shadow, he squeezed the brakes gently. The bicycle slowed, and his feet touched down. Xiaohe looked back. ‘I stopped it!’
After a few more glides, Xiaohe lifted his feet briefly. The bicycle wobbled. He put his feet down at once and stood steadily again.
‘That felt a little scary,’ he said. Dad asked, ‘A rest, or another little glide?’ Xiaohe chose a drink of water.
Next time, Xiaohe began with gliding again. The tree's shadow had shifted farther away, and his glides grew a little longer too.
He put one foot on a pedal. ‘Could you hold the seat for a little while?’ Dad agreed. ‘I'll tell you before I let go.’
One foot pressed down, and the other followed. The wheels turned forward. ‘I'm going to let go,’ Dad said. Xiaohe nodded.
After Dad let go, Xiaohe pedalled a few more turns. Before the shadow, he squeezed the brakes gently and put his feet down once he had stopped.
‘I can start, and I can stop!’ Xiaohe smiled. On his last turn that day, he simply practised stopping beside a fallen leaf.
After several more practices, Dad set out two soft markers with a wide curve between them. Xiaohe walked the route, pushing his bicycle first.
He rode slowly toward the bend, looking where he wanted to go. The handlebar turned little by little, without a sudden twist.
The first time, he stopped early. The second time, the wheels curved around the marker and returned to Dad. ‘I rode around that bend!’
Xiaohe pointed at the gate. ‘Can we ride outside one day?’ ‘When we're ready, we'll find a suitable place,’ Dad said. ‘I'll come with you.’
Before going home, he rode around the wide curve once more and stopped beside Dad. The bell rang softly. This little journey was complete.
yong-chi-li-de-yi-xiao-duan: The pool water shimmered. Duoduo put on her swimming cap and held Mama's hand. ‘I want to learn, but there's so much water.’
Her teacher welcomed her and showed her the poolside. ‘Wait for an adult to go into the water with you. Walk slowly here; don't run.’
Duoduo sat at the edge with her feet in the water. Her teacher stood in front of her in the pool, watching her toes turn into little blurry shadows.
‘It's cool.’ Duoduo pulled her feet back, then put them in again. Her teacher waited without pulling her into the water.
When she was ready, Duoduo held the rail and walked down the steps. Her teacher stayed beside her, and the water reached around her waist.
She cupped a little water and blew small ripples. ‘There's no hurry to put your face in,’ her teacher said. ‘Let's get to know the water first.’
Duoduo watched her teacher bring her mouth near the surface and breathe out little bubbles. ‘Do the bubbles come out of your mouth?’ she asked.
She tried too, but a splash touched her nose. Duoduo lifted her head at once. ‘I'd like to wipe my face.’ Her teacher offered a little towel.
That day, she tried bubbles just a few times, then rested outside the pool. She told Mama, ‘Today I had a little conversation with the water.’
At the next lesson, the bubbles came more easily. Duoduo held the pool edge and tried gently moving her legs with her teacher's help.
At first, her feet sent splashes high into the air. Her teacher supported her and showed smaller movements. Duoduo slowly found a less tiring kick.
After a few more lessons, her teacher brought a yellow pool noodle. ‘Would you like to feel your body float today, or practise kicking at the edge again?’
Duoduo chose the noodle. Her teacher placed it carefully and supported her close by. As her feet left the floor, Duoduo said, ‘Please keep holding me first.’
‘I'm right here,’ her teacher said. Duoduo kicked gently. The yellow noodle moved, and her body moved forward a little too.
She stopped and stood on the pool floor to catch her breath. ‘Even little movements can help me go forward.’
On her last turn, Duoduo used the noodle and swam a short way with her teacher protecting her close by. At the edge, she held on firmly first.
When Mama came to collect her, Duoduo pointed at that little stretch. ‘Today my legs brought me over there. My teacher stayed beside me.’
She folded her cap into the bag. ‘Next time, I'll wait for my teacher before getting in again.’ The yellow towel looked like a little piece of sunshine.
zhi-fei-ji-fei-guo-lan-xian: Grandma opened a drawer and took out some pale-yellow paper. ‘Did you fold planes when you were little?’ Anan asked. Grandma smiled and nodded.
Grandma folded one first. Anan held her sheet up. ‘I want to make my own. It doesn't have to fly very far.’
She folded the long sheet in half, but the corners did not quite meet. When she pressed down, a crooked crease stayed behind.
‘First, let's see if the edges meet,’ Grandma said, showing her slowly. Anan opened the paper and brought its edges together like two little doors closing.
One corner kept sliding away. ‘Could you hold this part while I press?’ Anan asked. Grandma rested a finger lightly on the corner.
A clear line appeared down the middle. Anan folded the top corners toward it. One arrived, but the other was still halfway there.
She paused and moved the unfinished corner closer. At last, two little triangles stood shoulder to shoulder beside the middle line.
Following Grandma's slow steps, Anan made the paper narrower and folded it together. She opened one wing, then the other.
Her first plane had one wing high and one wing low. Anan still wanted to try. ‘Let's see how it flies first.’
They put a strip of blue tape across the empty hallway. Grandma checked there was nobody ahead, then Anan gently launched the plane into the clear space.
The plane tilted sideways and landed before the blue line. Anan picked it up instead of throwing it away. ‘Why did it go this way?’
Grandma invited her to hold it level. Anan looked from behind. ‘This side is lower, and that side is bigger.’
She made the wings nearly the same height and tried again. The plane still missed the line, but it no longer turned sharply sideways.
‘That was different!’ Anan said. She took a fresh sheet, deciding to line up both sides carefully from the start.
Corners, creases, and two wings: she checked each one slowly. Grandma's hands rested in her lap. This time, the paper needed no helping finger.
The new plane left Anan's hand, passed the blue line, and glided toward the far end of the hallway. Anan stayed where she was and laughed with delight.
She placed both planes side by side. ‘This one taught me to look at the wings. That one taught me to line things up.’ Grandma asked what she would name them.
Anan thought. ‘They're both Anan One. I made them.’ She found another sheet. This time, she wanted to try a pair of wider wings.
